explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. David says, "You have set Your glory above the heavens." (Psalm 8:1) Think about how high the sky goes, and then think about God's glory sitting ABOVE all of that. I get a sore neck just picturing it.

Mount Zion is a real place, friend, but David doesn't mention it in this psalm. He says, "You have set Your glory above the heavens." (Psalm 8:1) So his eyes are pointed way higher than any mountain. Way, way higher.

Nice try, friend, but the Jordan River never shows up in this psalm. David says, "You have set Your glory above the heavens." (Psalm 8:1) The heavens are a lot bigger than one river. That's a whole lot of sky to put glory over.
Yes, friend! David says, "From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise…" (Psalm 8:2) Little ones with tiny voices, and God picks THEM. I love that so much.

Priests and Levites served in Israel's worship, but David doesn't name them here. He says, "From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise…" (Psalm 8:2) The voices God picks are the smallest ones. I didn't see that coming either.

I get why you'd think kings, friend. David was a king himself. But he says, "From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise…" (Psalm 8:2) God doesn't pick the loudest voices in the palace. He picks the littlest ones.

That's the word, friend. David says the praise is to "silence the enemy and avenger." (Psalm 8:2) God's enemies get quiet, and the praise comes from little ones. I'd pay good money to see that moment.

Scatter sounds like a strong word, friend, but it's not the one David uses. He says the praise is "to silence the enemy and avenger." (Psalm 8:2) The enemy goes quiet, not running in every direction. Only one of those needs no sweeping up after.
Warn is a decent guess, friend, but David doesn't say it. The text says the praise is "to silence the enemy and avenger." (Psalm 8:2) The enemy and avenger don't get a warning. They get silence.

explanations.answer: What is man that You care for him
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. David asks, "what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?" (Psalm 8:4) He's looking at the moon and the stars and wondering why God cares about us. I think David was a little amazed, and I'd be too.

explanations.answer: Why do the wicked prosper on the earth
explanations.explanation: That question is a real one, friend, but you'll find it in another psalm, not this one. In Psalm 8, David asks, "what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?" (Psalm 8:4) He's looking up at the sky, and the question that comes out is about how much God cares for us.

explanations.answer: How long will You hide Your face from me
explanations.explanation: David does ask that in Psalm 13:1, friend, but this isn't that psalm. Here he looks up at the sky and asks, "what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?" (Psalm 8:4) This question is full of wonder, not worry.
True, friend! David says, "You made him a little lower than the angels…" (Psalm 8:5) Under that giant sky, we end up close to the angels. I wouldn't have guessed it either.

It's actually true, friend. David says, "You made him a little lower than the angels…" (Psalm 8:5) The sky makes us look tiny, but God places us right up near the angels. Don't let the stars talk you out of that.
Ruler is right, friend. David says, "You made him ruler of the works of Your hands…" (Psalm 8:6) That's a big job to hand to people. I can barely rule over one oven timer.
I see why servant came to mind, friend, but it's not the word David uses. He says, "You made him ruler of the works of Your hands…" (Psalm 8:6) That's a promotion, not a uniform.

Stranger is a bit of a sad word, friend, and David doesn't use it. He says, "You made him ruler of the works of Your hands…" (Psalm 8:6) Man isn't a stranger to God's creation. He's put in charge of it.

I can see why you'd say that, friend, but the list keeps going. After the land animals, David adds, "the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, all that swim the paths of the seas." (Psalm 8:8) So it goes up to the sky and down into the water. David wasn't done yet.

Right, friend, it doesn't stop on land. David starts with "all sheep and oxen, and even the beasts of the field," and then adds "the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, all that swim the paths of the seas." (Psalm 8:7-8) The list covers the land, the sky and the water. Nothing gets left out.
